extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Alice/Mayo two-step framework (35 U.S.C. §101) including considerations such as improvements to technology, the machine-or-transformation clue, particular transformations, and whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to any other technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in technology beyond mere computer functionality may demonstrate patent eligibility; claims directed to an improvement in a technological process (rather than to an abstract idea) can be eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should describe how the claimed invention improves the existing technology (e.g., McRO: particular rules that enabled automation of specific animation tasks). To show an improvement, claims must recite details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to performance. Merely adding generic computer components or instructions to perform the method on generic machinery is not sufficient. Examples of sufficient improvements include particular computerized methods for rubber molding (Diehr), new telephone/server combos (TLI), improved downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV), improved digital compression (DDR Holdings), new data-generating measurement devices (Electric Power Group), specific sensor configurations (Thales Visionix), specific structured GUIs (Trading Techs), and improved biomedical preservation processes (CellzDirect). Examples of insufficient improvements include commonplace business methods on general-purpose computers (Alice), routine laboratory techniques, gathering/analyzing/displaying information by conventional techniques (TLI), high-level delivery of broadcast content to portable devices, general email screening on generic computers, and selecting existing content/functions from known options (Affinity Labs). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and § 2106.05(f) for more on mere instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation is a useful clue but not standalone
rubrics_metrics.description: "The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue, and investigative tool" for §101 eligibility, but it is not a stand-alone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claims must be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part test. If a claim passes Alice/Mayo (not directed to an exception at Step 2A or amounts to significantly more at Step 2B), it is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test. Conversely, a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test. Examiners can use the M-or-T test as an investigative tool but must still apply the two-step framework. See Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the elements of the machine/apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering whether a claimed machine provides significantly more than a judicial exception, assess the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (not any and all machines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recitation of particular machine structure (e.g., antenna shape/length in Mackay Radio; Fourdrinier machine components in Eibel Process) can indicate a particular machine. By contrast, a general purpose computer that applies an exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial; TLI). Merely reciting concrete or tangible components is not an inventive concept. If an applicant adds a generic computer or generic components and asserts they make the claim 'specially programmed' or a 'particular machine,' the examiner should determine whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception; adding generic computer components or programming to perform generic functions does not automatically overcome eligibility rejections. See MPEP § 2106.03 and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine implements the steps of the method (integral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the machine is used integrally to achieve performance of the claimed method (plays a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed) rather than merely being an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine cannot perform the claimed method steps (e.g., the Internet cannot itself perform fraud detection steps in CyberSource), mere recitation of the Internet or other machines as data sources or objects will not provide significantly more. Additional elements that invoke computers or machinery merely as tools to perform an existing process generally will not be significantly more. See CyberSource and Versata (machine must permit performance, not solely speed up an obvious solution). See MPEP § 2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether machine involvement is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine solely for data-gathering steps, or as a field-of-use limitation, typically does not provide significantly more (Bilski; CyberSource). If the machine contributes only nominally to the execution of claimed steps, it will not render an otherwise ineligible claim eligible. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation (transformation of an article to a different state or thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing is a clue that the claim may be significantly more than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of an article (physical object or substance) to a different state or thing is an indicator of patentability for process claims not tied to particular machines, but it is not a stand-alone test. Data manipulation alone (mere mathematical constructs) is not considered an eligible transformation. See Bilski, Diamond v. Diehr, CyberSource, Tilghman v. Proctor. Consider the particularity of the transformation, particularity of the article, nature/extent of change, nature of the article, and whether the transformation is merely extra-solution or field-of-use. See MPEP § 2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how definite or particular the recited transformation is; more particular transformations are more likely to provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing, smelting) show transformations using chemical/physical acts that are sufficiently definite to confine the patent monopoly. A more particular transformation (specific chemical/physical acts and parameters) is likely to weigh toward eligibility. See Gottschalk v. Benson discussion of Corning v. Burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: degree to which the recited article is particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the transformation is applied to a specifically identified article versus a generically recited article; transformations of generically recited articles are less likely to provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation limited to particular, specifically identifiable articles is more likely to provide significantly more; transformations claimed over 'any and all' articles are less persuasive. Specific identification of the article supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: nature of the transformation (type/extent of change in state or thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the transformation results in a different function or use of the article (likely significant) versus merely a change in location (unlikely significant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations that alter function/use (e.g., raw uncured rubber to precision-molded products) are more likely to provide significantly more; mere relocation or trivial change is not. See Diamond v. Diehr example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: nature of the article transformed (physical vs intangible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations of physical or tangible objects/substances are more likely to provide significantly more than transformations of intangible concepts (contracts, mental judgments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical/tangible transformations weigh toward eligibility; manipulation of purely mental constructs or intangible subject matter does not. For data, mere manipulation of mathematical constructs is not a qualifying transformation. See CyberSource and Warmerdam citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation factor: whether transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed transformation merely limits the claim to a particular field-of-use or is nominal/insignificant to executing the claimed method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the transformation contributes only nominally (e.g., merely administering a drug as a field-of-use limitation in Mayo), it will not provide significantly more. See Mayo analysis where Supreme Court found administering the drug was only a field-of-use limitation and insufficient to confer eligibility. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry; if so (and recited at a high level), they do not favor eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are specific limitations beyond what is well-understood/routine/conventional (e.g., unconventional steps confining the claim to a particular useful application), then they favor eligibility (DDR Holdings example). If additional elements are merely well-known routine activities (e.g., measuring metabolites by any known process in Mayo), they will not amount to an inventive concept. This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere-instruction, and insignificant-extra-solution considerations. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) and case law (DDR Holdings; Mayo; Parker v. Flook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative point: an element known in the art can still be unconventional/non-routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Known-in-the-art elements are not automatically routine; novelty/obviousness is separate from eligibility — elements known in the art can still be unconventional in how they are used and thus favor eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not conflate novelty/obviousness with eligibility. Example: Enfish claims reflected an improvement in database technology (self-referential table features) that were considered unconventional for purposes of eligibility even though anticipated by a prior art reference. Thus, an element taught in the prior art can still be non-routine in context and favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative point: prior art search is not required to decide routine/conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner need not perform a prior art search to determine whether an additional element is well-understood, routine, and conventional; reliance should be on what courts or those in the art recognize as widely prevalent or in common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner should conclude an element is well-understood, routine, conventional only when they can readily conclude, based on their expertise in the art, that the element is widely prevalent or commonly used in the relevant industry. If not widely prevalent or otherwise beyond elements recognized by courts or the art, the element will typically favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Alice/Mayo two-step test for all claims
rubrics_metrics.description: All claims must be evaluated using the two-part Alice/Mayo framework: Step 2A — determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception; Step 2B — determine whether the claim recites significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is not directed to an exception at Step 2A or amounts to significantly more at Step 2B, it is eligible. If it is directed to an exception at Step 2A and does not amount to significantly more at Step 2B, it is ineligible. Use other Step 2B considerations (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use) to inform the analysis. See Alice/Mayo decisions and MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B considerations to evaluate 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether claimed elements provide significantly more than a judicial exception, consider: mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use/technological environment, and the definition/role of a 'machine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may find it helpful to evaluate MPEP § 2106.05(f) (mere instructions to apply an exception), § 2106.05(g) (insignificant extra-solution activity), and § 2106.05(h) (field of use/technological environment) in determining whether an element or combination of elements makes a claim significantly more than the judicial exception. Also consider MPEP § 2106.03 for the definition of 'machine.'
